narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 50.8% probability that you would fail the bar exam on the first attempt. That is just over half, so this was not a high-certainty prediction, but it was enough for the model to rank failure as more likely than passing.

The strongest factor in that decision was your undergraduate GPA of 3.40, which is above the 3.23 average for accepted students and therefore pushed your prediction toward passing. However, the next two most influential factors both pushed toward failure: your third-year class decile of 2, then your first-year class decile of 2. Accepted students averaged about 5.79 in the third-year decile and 6.00 in the first-year decile, so your much lower class standing in both years weighed heavily against you, especially in the third year. Your LSAT score of 33, below the accepted-student average of 37.18, is another area to strengthen, though it was not among the top three drivers.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic profile: seek advising about why your class standing was low, consider additional coursework or academic support, and retake the LSAT if you can improve your score. You may also ask whether the school allows you to explain circumstances and reapply after showing stronger evidence of bar-exam readiness.
